children: Anthropic is moving forward with preparations for a potentially major initial public offering, even as its chief executive, Dario Amodei, has called for stronger safeguards and a slower pace of development for some advanced artificial intelligence systems, according to reporting by

The AI company, which develops the Claude chatbot, is projected to generate more than $100B in annualized revenue this year, according to people familiar with its finances cited by the Times. That figure would represent a significant increase from the roughly $65B annualized revenue reported in July.

The strong growth has fueled expectations among investors that Anthropic could command a valuation of as much as $2 trillion in a public offering. According to people familiar with the company's plans, Anthropic could file financial documents related to the IPO in the coming weeks, potentially allowing its shares to begin trading as early as November.

The potential IPO comes as the AI industry faces growing scrutiny over the risks posed by increasingly powerful models. Amodei has recently advocated additional safeguards around AI development, adding to an ongoing debate over how quickly the technology should advance.

Going public would provide Anthropic with access to substantial amounts of capital at a time when the company faces enormous computing expenses. Investors expect Anthropic to have access to about five gigawatts of computing capacity by the end of this year and potentially double that amount by the end of 2027, according to people familiar with the figures. Such capacity would place it broadly alongside rival OpenAI.

Anthropic has also been actively engaging with potential investors. The company recently hosted roughly 100 venture capital investors at its San Francisco headquarters for an event focused on its technology and products. Several Anthropic executives and co-founders participated, along with AI researcher Andrej Karpathy, who joined the company this year after previously co-founding OpenAI.

During meetings with prospective investors, Anthropic has emphasized potential benefits of AI, including applications in biology and medical research. The company has also sought to reassure investors about competition from lower-cost, open-weight AI models developed in China, arguing that only a relatively small share of businesses currently depend on those systems, according to the Times' sources.

Some investors believe Anthropic can continue expanding even if it slows development in certain areas. Much of its revenue comes from businesses using Claude, and corporate adoption of generative AI remains at an early stage.

At the same time, the IPO could present unusual challenges. Lawyers and bankers cited by the Times said Anthropic is entering largely unfamiliar territory because of the potential legal and financial consequences associated with advanced AI systems. Questions have also been raised about how the company could balance AI safety objectives with the growth expectations that typically accompany being a publicly traded company.
Anthropic's governance structure could provide some protection for its safety-focused mission, but going public would bring greater financial disclosure and scrutiny.

The company's plans also contrast with those of OpenAI. The Times reported that OpenAI's chief executive, Sam Altman, recently said the company was postponing a potential public offering until 2027 as it continues efforts to strengthen its finances and pursue a much higher valuation.

For Anthropic, that could create an opportunity to enter the public markets before its larger rival. However, the company has not finalized the timing of its offering, and the plans remain subject to change.

title: Anthropic advances IPO plans as AI safety debate intensifies
